newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein trawls votes in key N.Irish poll seat.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein trawls votes in key N.Irish poll seat.

text.p: As an Irish flag flew defiantly close to a British army base, top Sinn Fein official Martin McGuinness campaigned for Catholic votes and blamed Britain for blocking peace in Northern Ireland.
The senior strategist of the political arm of IRA pumped home his message on the doorsteps in a bid to get Catholics to close ranks and give him a landmark victory in Britain's May 1 election.

While heavily back-packed British troops warily patrolled this market town's main street, shirt-sleeved McGuinness breezed through a Catholic district predicting national defeat for Prime Minister John Major and the possibility of a fresh peace drive.

Trying to win Mid-Ulster, one of the province's 18 parliamentary seats, McGuinness told young and old alike he was best placed to unseat the pro-British Protestant "Unionist". But primarily, Sinn Fein was contesting seats to try and rebuild peace hopes by winning a ticket to talks, he argued.
"Major destroyed the first peace process. He put obstacle after obstacle in the way of talks," McGuinness told a young woman who had a child by her side.
"He's going to lose this election. There's going to be a new British government, and I see that as a new opportunity for the peace (process).
"It is also the best opportunity the nationalist people will ever have to get rid of (incumbent) Willie McCrea."

To Britain, Sinn Fein is the voluble Siamese twin of the clandestine Irish Republican Army which last year ended a lengthy cease-fire and relaunched a bomb and bullet campaign against London's sovereignty over the province.

Backed by the Irish government in a peace process that has floundered amid guerrilla strife and inter-communal conflict, Britain says the IRA must call a truce before Sinn Fein will be allowed into talks.

Sinn Fein, which says it can score a breakthrough and win three seats, claims London squandered the opportunities of the IRA's initial 17 month cease-fire by reneging on a deal of a fast track to talks.
"If I get elected here and (Sinn Fein president) Gerry (Adams) gets elected in Belfast...it makes it very difficult for them (Britain) to keep us out," McGuinness told an old man.

In the heart of Mid-Ulster, and the rest of the province, the election is about the future of British rule and how to achieve peace. On the Catholic housing estate, no one asked McGuinness about anything else.
"You've my vote," a woman assured him.
But the province's Protestants despise him as a former convicted guerrilla turned political activist who wants to turn their world upside down by ending British rule.
They hope the Catholic vote will split evenly and allow McCrea, a fundamentalist cleric and local gospel-song recording star, to hold it for the hard-line Democratic Unionist Party.

The main Catholic moderate party, Social Democratic and Labour (SDLP) insists it will hold its current four seats and beat off challenges from McGuinness, party leader Adams and Sinn Fein vice-president Pat Doherty.
Catholic voters who supported Sinn Fein in province-wide elections last year feel duped that it did not deliver an IRA cease-fire, the SDLP says.

The SDLP says it will have no truck with Sinn Fein in electoral pacts while the IRA remains at war and Sinn Fein holds to a policy of refusing to occupy seats in the British parliament, even if elected, in protest against rule from London.
